# OPENING: The Standard Reading

**Position.** Christ had no biological father. By "biological father" I mean a human male who supplied the seed from which the child was conceived. The KJV text says the child was conceived in Mary by the Holy Ghost, with no man involved. Joseph was Mary's husband and the child's reputed, legal father, and he was not the begetter.

I take the chain as the unit. Each link below rests on its own footing, and the conclusion rests on the links together.

---

## I. The genealogy stops saying "begat" at the one place it matters

**[L1]** Matthew 1:2-16 runs by one formula: "Abraham begat Isaac; and Isaac begat Jacob…" At the last link the formula changes: "Jacob begat Joseph the husband of Mary, of whom was born Jesus, who is called Christ" (Matt 1:16).

**[L2]** The verb in the repeated formula is ἐγέννησεν (*egennēsen*, "he begat / fathered"), active, with a male subject. Verse 16 says Joseph is τὸν ἄνδρα Μαρίας (*ton andra Marias*, "the husband of Mary"), not the one who begat. It then switches to ἐξ ἧς ἐγεννήθη (*ex hēs egennēthē*, "out of whom was born"). The verb is passive, and the relative pronoun ἧς (*hēs*, "whom") is feminine singular. The antecedent can only be Mary, so the birth is traced to her alone.

**[L3]** Luke 3:23 agrees by saying Jesus was "being (as was supposed) the son of Joseph." The genealogy's own grammar marks that supposition as not the fact.

## II. The text names the source of the conception

**[L1]** "When as his mother Mary was espoused to Joseph, before they came together, she was found with child of the Holy Ghost" (Matt 1:18). The angel says: "that which is conceived in her is of the Holy Ghost" (Matt 1:20). Gabriel says: "The Holy Ghost shall come upon thee, and the power of the Highest shall overshadow thee: therefore also that holy thing which shall be born of thee shall be called the Son of God" (Luke 1:35).

**[L2]** Matthew 1:18 says ἐν γαστρὶ ἔχουσα ἐκ πνεύματος ἁγίου (*en gastri echousa ek pneumatos hagiou*, "having in womb out of Spirit holy"). Matthew 1:20 says τὸ γὰρ ἐν αὐτῇ γεννηθὲν ἐκ πνεύματός ἐστιν ἁγίου (*to gar en autē gennēthen ek pneumatos estin hagiou*, "for that which is begotten in her is out of Spirit holy"). Both use the preposition ἐκ (*ek*, "out of"), which names the source. Luke 1:35 uses ἐπισκιάσει (*episkiasei*, "will overshadow"). It is a verb of divine presence, not of marital union.

**[L3]** The same Spirit that "moved upon the face of the waters" (Gen 1:2, Hebrew רוּחַ *ruach*, "spirit/breath") is the agent in creation. In Hebrews 10:5 the body is "prepared": σῶμα κατηρτίσω μοι (*sōma katērtisō moi*, "a body you fitted for me").

## III. No man was involved, by Mary's own statement and Matthew's

**[L1]** "Then said Mary unto the angel, How shall this be, seeing I know not a man?" (Luke 1:34). Joseph "knew her not till she had brought forth her firstborn son" (Matt 1:25). She was found with child "before they came together" (Matt 1:18).

**[L2]** The Greek of Luke 1:34 is ἐπεὶ ἄνδρα οὐ γινώσκω (*epei andra ou ginōskō*, "since a man I do not know"). The verb γινώσκω (*ginōskō*, "to know," used of marital relations) is in the present tense, and the question concerns how it can be so, given that. Matthew 1:18 uses πρὶν ἢ συνελθεῖν (*prin ē synelthein*, "before coming together"). Matthew 1:25 uses ἐγίνωσκεν… ἕως οὗ (*eginōsken… heōs hou*, "he knew [her] not until"), which marks the point up to which the birth had happened without him.

**[L3]** Joseph's reaction confirms it. He was "minded to put her away privily" (Matt 1:19), which shows he knew he was not the cause. The angel's word in Matthew 1:20 answers that suspicion: "fear not to take unto thee Mary thy wife."

## IV. The Scripture's own prophetic pattern requires it

**[L1]** "Therefore the Lord himself shall give you a sign; Behold, a virgin shall conceive, and bear a son, and shall call his name Immanuel" (Isa 7:14). Matthew applies it: "Behold, a virgin shall be with child, and shall bring forth a son" (Matt 1:22-23).

**[L2]** The Hebrew is הָעַלְמָה (*ha-almah*, "the young woman of marriageable age"). Matthew's Greek is παρθένος (*parthenos*, "virgin"). Isaiah calls it אוֹת (*oth*, "a sign"), and in context it was to be a sign "either in the depth, or in the height above" (Isa 7:11). An ordinary conception by a husband is no sign. The word *almah* is used of Rebekah in Genesis 24:43, and she is described in Genesis 24:16 as בְּתוּלָה (*bethulah*, "virgin") whom "no man had known." That shows the term can describe an unmarried young woman who has not known a man.

**[L3]** Genesis 3:15 speaks of the woman's seed: זַרְעָהּ (*zar'ah*, "her seed"). Seed is normally reckoned by the man, and here it is attributed to the woman. Galatians 4:4 echoes this with "made of a woman," γενόμενον ἐκ γυναικός (*genomenon ek gynaikos*, "come to be out of a woman").

**[L3]** The strongest cross-reference is Jeremiah 22:30. God says of Coniah (Jechonias): "no man of his seed shall prosper, sitting upon the throne of David." Hebrew זֶרַע (*zera*, "seed"). Matthew 1:11-12 places Jechonias in Joseph's line. If Joseph were the biological father, the child would be of Coniah's seed and barred from David's throne. Yet Luke 1:32 promises "the throne of his father David." The text is consistent only if the descent from David came through Mary and not by Joseph's begetting.

## V. Joseph is called "father" in a legal and reputed sense, and the child corrects the term

**[L1]** "Being (as was supposed) the son of Joseph" (Luke 3:23). "Is not this Jesus, the son of Joseph, whose father and mother we know?" (John 6:42), which is the crowd speaking. "Thy father and I have sought thee sorrowing" (Luke 2:48), which is Mary speaking, and the child answers: "wist ye not that I must be about my Father's business?" (Luke 2:49).

**[L2]** The word in Luke 3:23 is ἐνομίζετο (*enomizeto*, "was reckoned / supposed by custom"). It marks a reputation, not a fact. In Luke 2:49 the child's "my Father" (τοῦ πατρός μου, *tou patros mou*, "of the father of me") answers Mary's use of "thy father" and redirects it.

**[L3]** In Matthew 1:20 the angel does not call Joseph the father. Joseph is told to "take unto thee Mary thy wife," and in verse 21 "she shall bring forth a son, and thou shalt call his name JESUS." Joseph names the child, which is a legal act of acknowledging him. Matthew 1:25 says "he called his name JESUS."

## VI. Flesh-descent from David is accounted for without Joseph

**[L1]** "Made of the seed of David according to the flesh" (Rom 1:3). "Of the fruit of his loins, according to the flesh, he would raise up Christ to sit on his throne" (Acts 2:30).

**[L2]** Romans 1:3 says ἐκ σπέρματος Δαυὶδ κατὰ σάρκα (*ek spermatos David kata sarka*, "out of the seed of David according to flesh"). Galatians 4:4 says γενόμενον ἐκ γυναικός (*genomenon ek gynaikos*, "come to be out of a woman"). Combined with the Jeremiah 22:30 bar, flesh-descent from David is carried by the woman.

**[L4]** Mary is the only human parent the text names as the source of the child's body (Matt 1:16 *ex hēs*, "out of whom"; Gal 4:4 *ek gynaikos*, "out of a woman"). The text also states that David's flesh-line reaches him (Rom 1:3, Acts 2:30) and that Coniah's line is barred (Jer 22:30). Therefore the flesh-descent from David runs through Mary, and no male contributor is needed or named.

---

## DECLARED CHAIN -- the links your case stands on

1. Matthew 1:16 breaks the repeated "begat" formula (ἐγέννησεν, *egennēsen*, "he begat") and traces the birth to Mary alone: Joseph is τὸν ἄνδρα Μαρίας (*ton andra Marias*, "the husband of Mary"), and the birth is ἐξ ἧς ἐγεννήθη (*ex hēs egennēthē*, "out of whom was born," feminine singular). Footing: [L1] Matt 1:2-16; [L2] active versus passive verb and feminine relative pronoun; [L3] Luke 3:23.
2. The text names the source of the conception as the Holy Ghost and not a man: ἐκ πνεύματος ἁγίου (*ek pneumatos hagiou*, "out of Spirit holy"). Footing: [L1] Matt 1:18, 20; Luke 1:35; [L2] ἐκ (*ek*, "out of") and ἐπισκιάσει (*episkiasei*, "will overshadow"); [L3] Heb 10:5.
3. No man knew Mary before the conception, by her own word and Matthew's. Footing: [L1] Luke 1:34; Matt 1:18, 25; [L2] ἄνδρα οὐ γινώσκω (*andra ou ginōskō*, "a man I do not know") and πρὶν ἢ συνελθεῖν (*prin ē synelthein*, "before coming together"); [L3] Joseph's intent to "put her away privily," Matt 1:19.
4. The prophetic record requires a conception without a human father: a sign (Isa 7:14), the woman's seed (Gen 3:15), and the bar on Coniah's seed (Jer 22:30) set against the promised throne (Luke 1:32). Footing: [L1] Isa 7:14; Matt 1:23; Gen 3:15; Jer 22:30; [L2] עַלְמָה (*almah*, "young woman"), אוֹת (*oth*, "sign"), זֶרַע (*zera*, "seed"); [L3] Matt 1:11-12 with Gen 24:16, 43.
5. Joseph is called "father" only in the reputed and legal sense, and the child himself redirects the term to "my Father." Footing: [L1] Luke 3:23; Luke 2:48-49; John 6:42; Matt 1:21, 25; [L2] ἐνομίζετο (*enomizeto*, "was supposed") and τοῦ πατρός μου (*tou patros mou*, "of my Father"); [L3] Matt 1:20-21.
6. Therefore Christ had no biological father: he was conceived in Mary by the Holy Ghost, Mary alone supplied his human descent from David, and Joseph was her husband and his reputed, legal father only. Footing: [L1] Matt 1:16, 18, 20; Luke 1:34-35; Rom 1:3; [L2] ἐξ ἧς (*ex hēs*, "out of whom"), ἐκ γυναικός (*ek gynaikos*, "out of a woman"), ἐκ πνεύματος ἁγίου (*ek pneumatos hagiou*, "out of Spirit holy"); [L3] Jer 22:30 against Matt 1:11-12, Acts 2:30.

# ROUND 2: The Chain Stands

**Frame.** The question is who begat the child, and the case is the chain, not any single verse. Each verse the challenger raises goes back into its row. Every row he cites names *David's* body. None names *Joseph's* body as the source of the child.

---

## I. The keystone: "loins," "bowels," "seed," "flesh"

**[L1]** The challenger's rows are Acts 2:30, "of the fruit of his loins, according to the flesh, he would raise up Christ to sit on his throne"; Rom 1:3, "made of the seed of David according to the flesh"; and 2 Sam 7:12, "thy seed after thee, which shall proceed out of thy bowels." Each names **David** as the body. None says "Joseph begat Jesus."

**[L2]** ὀσφύς (*osphys*, "loins") is a descent word, not a word for the immediate begetter. Hebrews 7:10 puts Levi "yet in the loins of his father" when Melchisedec met Abraham, and Abraham was Levi's great-grandfather. In Hebrew, חֲלָצַיִם (*chalatsayim*, "loins") works the same way. **[L3]** Genesis 46:26 reads "all the souls that came with Jacob into Egypt, which came out of his loins, **besides Jacob's sons' wives**." Grandchildren, born through mothers, "came out of his loins." The idiom covers descent through intervening generations and through women. Acts 2:30 therefore requires David's flesh to reach the child. It does not require Joseph to be the begetter.

**[L2]** Romans 1:3 uses γενομένου (*genomenou*, "having come to be"), not the genealogy's ἐγέννησεν (*egennēsen*, "he begat"). It is the same verb Galatians 4:4 uses: γενόμενον ἐκ γυναικός (*genomenon ek gynaikos*, "come to be out of a woman"). **[L3]** The two verses interlock. David's flesh reaches the child, and the text says he came to be "out of a woman."

**[L4]** The inference is that Mary is the bearer of David's flesh. Footing: **[L1]** Matt 1:20 says what was begotten in her is "of the Holy Ghost," and Luke 1:35 says "that holy thing which shall be born of thee." **[L2]** Matt 1:16 has ἐξ ἧς (*ex hēs*, "out of whom," feminine). **[L3]** Rom 1:3 and Acts 2:30 state that David's flesh reaches him. Once the Spirit is the stated source (not a man) and the woman is the stated bearer, the elimination is complete. Noted that no verse prints "Mary, daughter of Heli." Not conceding here. Goes to review.

---

## II. Jeremiah 22:30

**[L1]** Jer 22:24 reads "Though Coniah… were the signet upon my right hand, yet would I pluck thee thence." Jer 22:30 reads "no man of his seed shall prosper, sitting upon the throne of David."

- **Jer 18:7-8** is the rule for a "nation… kingdom." Jer 22:30 states a decree on a man and records no turning. Verses 28-29 preface it with "O earth, earth, earth, hear the word of the LORD."
- **Haggai 2:23.** **[L1]** Hag 1:1 calls Zerubbabel "governor of Judah." He is a governor, not a king "sitting upon the throne." The signet promise in Haggai concerns the LORD's servant, and it does not place him on David's throne.
- **1 Chr 3:17-19** lists sons. A list of sons is not a throne. The bar says "prosper, sitting upon the throne," and it does not say "have children."
- **"Never cited in the New Testament."** That is an argument from silence. **[L1]** Matthew 1:11-12 itself puts Jechonias in Joseph's line, and Luke 1:32 promises "the throne of his father David."

**[L3]** The two registers diverge at David. Matt 1:6 reads "David the king begat Solomon." Luke 3:31 reads "Nathan, which was the son of David." Luke 3:27 has Zorobabel "the son of Salatiel, which was the son of **Neri**." Matthew's line passes through Jechonias and Luke's does not.

**[L4]** Matthew's line carries the legal right (Joseph, "thou son of David," Matt 1:20; the child named by him, 1:21, 25). Luke's line carries the flesh. Footing: **[L1]** Jer 22:30 against Matt 1:11-12; **[L2]** Luke 3:23 is τοῦ Ἠλί (*tou Eli*, "of Heli") with only the genitive article, so the Greek carries no verb "begat" and no noun "son" (the KJV's "the son" is supplied); **[L3]** Luke 3:27, 31 diverge from Matthew's line.

**Mary's kin.** **[L1]** Luke 1:36 calls Elisabeth Mary's "cousin," from συγγενής (*syngenēs*, "kinswoman"). Kinship across tribes is attested. **[L3]** Exod 6:23 reads "Aaron took him Elisheba, daughter of Amminadab" (Judah's prince's line, Num 1:7), and 2 Chr 22:11 has Jehoiada the priest marrying the king's daughter.

**Reckoning by the father.** Ezra 2:61-62 does not refuse the wife's house. **[L1]** The men "took a wife of the daughters of Barzillai… and was called after their name," and were put out "**because their register was not found**," not because of the wife. **[L3]** 1 Chr 2:21-22 has Segub born of Machir's daughter, and Num 32:41 calls his son "Jair the son of Manasseh." So the canon does reckon through a woman.

---

## III. Isaiah 7:14

**[L1]** Isa 7:13 reads "Hear ye now, O house of David," and 7:14 reads "the Lord himself shall give **you** a sign."

**[L2]** לָכֶם (*lākem*, "to you," plural) addresses the house of David. עַלְמָה (*almah*, "young woman") is a distinct word from בְּתוּלָה (*bethulah*, "virgin"), and I do not claim they are one word. **[L3]** Gen 24:16 calls Rebekah *bethulah* and says "neither had any man known her," and Gen 24:43 calls the same woman *ha-almah*, which the KJV renders "the virgin." So *almah* can designate a woman who has not known a man. **[L1]** Isa 7:11 sets the sign "either in the depth, or in the height above." A child conceived in the ordinary way by a husband is no such sign.

**[L1]** Matt 1:22-23 applies the text to this conception, and the challenger grants that "Matthew 1:23's application stands." **[L2]** Matthew's word is παρθένος (*parthenos*, "virgin"). The Isaiah 8:3 dating does not cancel Matthew's stated fulfilment, since a sign may have a near and a far reach.

---

## IV. Matthew 1 and Luke 1

**Matt 1:16.** **[L2]** The challenger says the passive "names no agent." But the genealogy has run on ἐγέννησεν (*egennēsen*, "begat") through the whole row, and at the one point where the verb would be expected, it is not used of Joseph. **[L1]** The text does say "Jacob begat Joseph the husband of Mary." It does not say "Joseph begat Jesus."

**Matt 1:20.** **[L2]** γεννηθέν (*gennēthen*) is the passive of γεννάω (*gennaō*, "to beget"), the same root as the genealogy's "begat." The text gives its source as ἐκ πνεύματος ἁγίου (*ek pneumatos hagiou*, "out of Spirit holy"). **[L1]** John 1:13 sets "of God" against "nor of the will of man." So the ἐκ (*ek*, "out of") of God stands in contrast to a man's begetting.

**Matt 1:18.** **[L1]** "Before they came together, she was found with child." **[L2]** πρὶν ἢ συνελθεῖν (*prin ē synelthein*, "before coming together"). The order is conception, then the finding, then the coming together. Whatever *synerchomai* means, the pregnancy was already there, so the conception did not come from that coming together. **[L1]** Matt 1:25 says "knew her not **till** she had brought forth," so no knowledge on Joseph's part is stated before the birth.

**Matt 1:19.** **[L4]** Joseph was "minded to put her away privily." Footing: **[L1]** 1:19-20, where the angel answers with "fear not to take unto thee Mary thy wife"; **[L3]** Deut 22:23-24, where the law treats a betrothed damsel's pregnancy by another man as a matter for judgment. A man who knew himself the father would have no reason to put her away. The angel's answer assumes Joseph's suspicion was real.

**Luke 1:34-35.** **[L1]** Luke 1:27 reads "a virgin espoused to a man whose name was Joseph," and Mary asks "How shall this be, seeing I know not a man?" **[L2]** The present ἄνδρα οὐ γινώσκω (*andra ou ginōskō*, "a man I do not know") is her state, and she is betrothed and expecting marriage. If an ordinary conception through Joseph were in view, the question would answer itself. **[L1]** The angel does not answer "Joseph will know thee." He answers "The Holy Ghost shall come upon thee… therefore also that holy thing… shall be called the Son of God." **[L3]** In contrast, Zacharias asked from natural means (Luke 1:18, "I am an old man") and was rebuked, while Mary's question was answered and she said "be it unto me according to thy word" (1:38).

**On ἐπέρχομαι and ἐπισκιάζω.** The challenger shows these verbs describe presence and power, and I agree. The "therefore" (**[L2]** διό, *dio*, "wherefore") grounds the title "Son of God" in that coming. No row puts a man's seed in that place.

---

## V. "Father" in the registers

**[L1]** John 6:42 reads "whose father and mother we know? how is it then that he saith, I came down from heaven?" The crowd's reckoning is the thing being corrected. **[L3]** John 7:27-28 has "we know this man whence he is," and the answer is "ye both know me, and ye know whence I am: and I am not come of myself, but he that sent me is true, whom ye know not."

**[L2]** ἐνομίζετο (*enomizeto*, "was reckoned") carries a reputation. Luke 3:23 itself brackets it as "(as was supposed)." **[L1]** Luke 1:3 says he wrote with "perfect understanding of all things from the very first," so Luke's parenthesis follows his own birth narrative. Mary's "thy father" in Luke 2:48 is the household's usage.

**[L3]** 1 Chr 28:6 has God's fatherhood given by choice ("I have chosen him to be my son") to a son David begat. Luke 1:35 has the Sonship grounded in the conception itself ("therefore also"). The two cases differ.

---
